lesson.title: fahren & its Dynasty
lesson.subtitle: The family tree reading — with the ablauf forms fuhr and gefahren

hook.title: The Tree, Read Aloud
hook.content: Yesterday I traveled to Berlin: Ich bin gestern nach Berlin gefahren. The journey was short: Die Fahrt war kurz. I did not drive a car — I rode the train: Ich bin mit dem Zug gefahren. The train departed at eight: Der Zug ist um acht abgefahren. Notice the dynasty working: fahren (the verb), gefahren (its participle), die Fahrt (the journey-noun), abgefahren (departed — the separable prefix rides ON the participle!). One root carries the whole travel story.

footnotes.title: Prefixes Ride on Participles
footnotes.content: Separable verbs form their participle with the prefix glued back on: abfahren → abgefahren (NOT ge-abfahrt). The ge- goes between prefix and stem: an+ge+kommen, auf+ge+standen. The prefix always wins first position.

pattern.title: The Travel Story Machine
pattern.content: The forms: fahren, fuhr, gefahren ↔ fare, fared. The Perfekt with sein: Ich bin gefahren (motion — no object), Ich habe das Auto gefahren (object — haben). The noun: die Fahrt (the journey), die Abfahrt (the departure), die Autofahrt (car ride — the compound law from topic 21 still works). The separable: abfahren, ist abgefahren. Reading plan: any German travel sentence is fahren + a preposition (nach + city, mit + vehicle) + a time word. You can now build all three parts.
pattern.linguist_note: Ich bin mit dem Zug gefahren — three systems in seven words: sein for motion, mit + dative (the mid-preposition!), and fahren's ablaut in the participle. The dynasty is the curriculum in miniature.

exercises.prompt: The dynasty in Perfekt — match each form with its meaning:
exercises.target_answer: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren, Der Zug ist abgefahren, Die Fahrt war kurz, Ich habe das Auto gefahren
exercises.explanation: Motion → sein; object → haben; the prefix rides the participle: ab-ge-fahren.

exercises.prompt: Why 'Ich BIN gefahren' but 'Ich HABE das Auto gefahren'?
options: Motion alone takes sein; a driven object brings haben back
exercises.target_answer: Motion alone takes sein; a driven object brings haben back
exercises.explanation: No object → sein (you moved). Object (das Auto) → haben (you did something to it). The choice gym's rule, alive in one verb.

exercises.prompt: Participle check: 'Der Zug ist um acht _____. ' (departed — abfahren):
exercises.explanation: ab + ge + fahren: the prefix takes first position, ge- slots inside, the ablaut stays.

exercises.prompt: What English word is the twin of 'Fahrt'?
exercises.explanation: Both from *faraną: English kept 'fare' for payment and 'farewell'; German kept Fahrt for the journey itself.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'Yesterday I traveled to Berlin by train'
exercises.target_answer: Gestern bin ich mit dem Zug nach Berlin gefahren
exercises.meaning: Yesterday I traveled to Berlin by train
exercises.explanation: Time (1), verb (2), subject (3), mit + dative, nach + city, participle last — the whole travel machine in one sentence.

summary.outcome: Narrate travel with fahren's dynasty: bin gefahren, ist abgefahren, die Fahrt.

use_example.german: Gestern bin ich mit dem Zug nach Berlin gefahren.
use_example.english: Yesterday I traveled to Berlin by train.

summary.takeaway: One root runs the railway: fahren/fuhr/gefahren, die Fahrt, abgefahren — motion takes sein, objects bring haben.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: ziehen & nehmen Dynasties — the tow/tug root and the nim root radiate too.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We drive / fare here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir fahren heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in fahren & its Dynasty.

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

fahrt.etymology_derivation: Noun of fahren (fare): a 'faring' — a drive, ride, or voyage; the -t is the Germanic -þ nominal suffix. [wiktionary]

zug.etymology_derivation: Noun of ziehen (to pull — the tow/tug family): a train is 'the pull(er)', an elevator the Aufzug ('up-pull'). [wiktionary]

aus.context_translation: I come from / out of Berlin.

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

frühling.etymology_derivation: A 15th-century formation from früh (early) + -ling; English spring is a different word — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

sonne.etymology_derivation: Old High German sunna — shares Proto-Germanic *sun(n)uz with English sun. [wiktionary]

haut.context_phrase: Die Haut brennt in der Sonne.
haut.context_translation: The skin burns in the sun.
haut.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūdiz — the twin of English hide (and Dutch huid). [wiktionary]

preis.etymology_derivation: Ultimately from Latin pretium — the same source as English price (and prize). [wiktionary]

mais.context_translation: The corn grows in the garden.
mais.etymology_derivation: From Spanish maíz, from Taíno mahis; English maize is the same borrowing, while corn is the everyday English name. [wiktionary]

faul.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fūlaz 'rotten, putrid' — the twin of English foul, which the page lists as a cognate; German diphthongized the vowel, and the sense slid from rotten to lazy, idleness as moral rot. [wiktionary]

lunge.context_phrase: Rauchen ist schlecht für die Lunge.
lunge.context_translation: Smoking is bad for the lungs.
lunge.etymology_derivation: From Old High German lunga, from Proto-Germanic *lungô, literally the light organ. English lung is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

krankheit.etymology_derivation: Krank (sick) plus -heit (-ness); the suffix -heit is the twin of English -hood (both Proto-Germanic *haiduz), so structurally sick-hood. [wiktionary]

zimt.context_phrase: Ich streue Zimt auf den Reis.
zimt.context_translation: I sprinkle cinnamon on the rice.
zimt.etymology_derivation: From Latin cinnamon, cinnamomum, through Greek kinnamomon, a Phoenician trade word per Herodotus; English cinnamon is a doublet of the same ancient spice word. [wiktionary]

schießen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skeutaną — English shoot is the documented cognate (Old English scēotan); strong verb: schoss, geschossen. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
